config.title: On-call & incident culture

intro.title: On-call & incident culture
intro.body: In this lesson, you will explore the fundamentals of on-call and incident culture in software engineering. You will learn how to structure an incident response process, including roles, communication channels, and post-mortem analysis. The core concepts involve understanding operational workflows and implementing structured documentation. You will engage with key leadership constructs like escalation policies, blameless retrospectives, and service-level objectives (SLOs). This beginner-friendly lesson focuses on building a solid foundation in managing live-site incidents effectively.
intro.usecase: This lesson's concepts are directly applied in the incident management dashboards and on-call coordination tools used by engineering teams at companies like Google, Amazon, and Netflix. For example, a real-time status dashboard displaying active incidents, a paging/alerting system interface for on-call engineers, and a post-mortem documentation form are all concrete UIs built upon these principles. As a developer, you might implement or customize these systems to display severity levels, assign responders, and log timeline events during an outage. Understanding this culture ensures you can build reliable, transparent tooling that helps teams respond quickly, learn from failures, and maintain service health.

objectives: Construct an on-call rotation schedule using a calendar-based configuration
Configure incident severity levels and corresponding response time targets
Implement an incident communication workflow with stakeholder notifications
Apply post-incident review templates to document root cause analysis
Integrate monitoring alerts with on-call escalation policies
Manipulate incident timelines to visualize response and resolution phases
Initialize an incident command structure with defined roles and responsibilities

steps.title: Import React and useState
steps.instruction: Import React and useState from 'react' to enable component creation and state management for the incident management interface.
steps.hint: Write the import statement at the top of your file. You'll need both React and the useState hook.
steps.analogousExample:
// Importing React and hooks for a component
import React, { useState } from 'react';
steps.expectedOutcome: The file will have the necessary imports to create React components with state management capabilities.
successCriteria: React and useState are imported from 'react'.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully imported React and useState. This gives you the foundation to build React components with state management.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close, but make sure you're importing both React and useState from 'react'. Check your import statement syntax.
steps.feedbackWrong: The imports aren't quite right. Remember to import both React and useState from the 'react' package.

steps.title: Create the IncidentCulture component
steps.instruction: Create a functional component named IncidentCulture that returns an empty div element.
steps.hint: Define a component that returns JSX. You can use either a function declaration or arrow function syntax.
steps.seedCode:
import React, { useState } from 'react';

// Create the IncidentCulture component here
steps.expectedOutcome: The component IncidentCulture is defined and returns an empty div.
successCriteria: A functional component named IncidentCulture exists and returns an empty div element.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've created the main component structure for the incident culture lesson.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close. Make sure you've defined a component named IncidentCulture that returns an empty div.
steps.feedbackWrong: The component isn't defined correctly. Check that you've created a functional component named IncidentCulture that returns an empty div.

steps.title: Initialize incident status state
steps.instruction: Inside your IncidentCulture component, initialize a state variable called incidentStatus using useState, setting its initial value to 'stable'.
steps.hint: Use the useState hook you imported earlier to create state that tracks the current incident status.
steps.expectedOutcome: The component will have a state variable incidentStatus initialized to 'stable' that can be used to track incident status changes.
successCriteria: The incidentStatus state variable is declared using useState with initial value 'stable'.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully initialized the incident status state. This will allow the component to track and respond to changes in incident status.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure you're using useState to create a state variable called incidentStatus with initial value 'stable'.
steps.feedbackWrong: The incident status state hasn't been initialized correctly. Remember to use useState to create a state variable called incidentStatus with initial value 'stable'.

steps.title: Initialize on-call engineer state
steps.instruction: Inside your IncidentCulture component, initialize a state variable called 'onCallEngineer' using useState, with an initial value of 'Not assigned'.
steps.hint: Use the useState hook to create a state variable and its setter function. The initial value should be the string 'Not assigned'.
steps.analogousExample:
// Similar: state for a team member
const [teamLead, setTeamLead] = useState('Unassigned');
steps.expectedOutcome: The component will have a state variable 'onCallEngineer' initialized to 'Not assigned', ready to track the current on-call engineer.
successCriteria: The state variable 'onCallEngineer' is declared with useState, initialized to 'Not assigned'.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully set up state to track the on-call engineer information.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close. Make sure you're using useState to declare a state variable named 'onCallEngineer' with the initial value 'Not assigned'.
steps.feedbackWrong: Let's try again. You need to initialize a state variable called 'onCallEngineer' with useState, setting it to 'Not assigned'.

steps.title: Define startIncident handler
steps.instruction: Inside your IncidentCulture component, define a function called handleStartIncident that sets incidentStatus to 'active' and onCallEngineer to 'Alex (Primary)'.
steps.hint: Create a function that updates both state variables when called. Use the setter functions from useState.
steps.expectedOutcome: The component now has a handler function that will update both state variables to simulate starting an incident.
successCriteria: A function named handleStartIncident is defined that calls setIncidentStatus('active') and setOnCallEngineer('Alex (Primary)').
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've created the incident start handler. This function will be triggered later to simulate initiating an incident response.
steps.feedbackPartial: You've defined a function, but make sure it updates both state variables: incidentStatus to 'active' and onCallEngineer to 'Alex (Primary)'.
steps.feedbackWrong: The handler function isn't defined correctly. Create a function called handleStartIncident that sets both state variables as specified.

steps.title: Define resolveIncident handler
steps.instruction: In your IncidentCulture component, define a function called handleResolveIncident that sets incidentStatus to 'resolved' and onCallEngineer back to 'Not assigned'.
steps.hint: Create a function that updates both state variables using their setter functions.
steps.expectedOutcome: The component will have a handleResolveIncident function that properly updates both state variables when called.
successCriteria: A function named handleResolveIncident is defined that sets incidentStatus to 'resolved' and onCallEngineer to 'Not assigned'.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've created the incident resolution handler. This function simulates the process of resolving an incident and freeing up the on-call engineer.
steps.feedbackPartial: You've defined a function, but it needs to update both state variables correctly. Make sure it sets incidentStatus to 'resolved' and onCallEngineer to 'Not assigned'.
steps.feedbackWrong: The function isn't defined correctly. Create a function called handleResolveIncident that updates both state variables as specified.

steps.title: Add component structure and title
steps.instruction: Replace the null return value with a container div containing an h1 element with the text 'On-call & Incident Culture'
steps.hint: Return JSX with a div wrapper and an h1 heading inside it.
steps.expectedOutcome: The component now returns a basic UI structure with a title heading.
successCriteria: The component returns a div containing an h1 element with the exact text 'On-call & Incident Culture'
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've created the basic UI structure with the appropriate title for the incident culture lesson.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure you're returning a div with an h1 element containing the exact text 'On-call & Incident Culture'.
steps.feedbackWrong: The component should return a div containing an h1 element with the text 'On-call & Incident Culture'. Check your JSX syntax and the text content.

steps.title: Display incident status information
steps.instruction: In your component's return statement, add a paragraph element that displays the current incidentStatus state with the text 'Current Status: [status]'
steps.hint:
Use JSX to create a

element and embed the incidentStatus variable inside curly braces.
steps.analogousExample:
// Displaying a state value in JSX

Current value: {someState}
steps.expectedOutcome: The UI will show the current incident status (initially 'resolved') in a paragraph element.
successCriteria: A paragraph element displays 'Current Status: [status]' where [status] shows the incidentStatus state value.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! The incident status is now visible in the UI, which is essential for transparency during on-call situations.
steps.feedbackPartial: You've added a paragraph, but make sure it displays the incidentStatus variable correctly using curly braces.
steps.feedbackWrong: The paragraph element isn't displaying the incident status. Remember to use JSX syntax with curly braces to show the state value.

steps.title: Display on-call engineer information
steps.instruction: Add a paragraph element inside the component's return statement that displays the current onCallEngineer state with the text 'On-call Engineer: [engineer]'.
steps.hint:
Use JSX to create a

tag and embed the onCallEngineer state variable inside curly braces.
steps.analogousExample:
// Displaying a state variable in JSX

Current user: {username}
steps.expectedOutcome: The UI will show the current on-call engineer assignment below the incident status information.
successCriteria: A paragraph element displays the text 'On-call Engineer: ' followed by the current onCallEngineer state value.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully displayed the on-call engineer information, which is crucial for transparency during incident response.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close. Make sure your paragraph shows both the static text 'On-call Engineer: ' and the dynamic onCallEngineer value.
steps.feedbackWrong: The paragraph isn't displaying the on-call engineer information correctly. Check that you're using the onCallEngineer state variable inside JSX curly braces.

steps.title: Add incident control buttons with handlers
steps.instruction: Add two button elements inside the return statement: one with the text 'Start Incident' that calls handleStartIncident when clicked, and another with the text 'Resolve Incident' that calls handleResolveIncident when clicked.
steps.hint: Place the buttons after the existing paragraphs. Use the onClick attribute to connect each button to its corresponding handler function.
steps.expectedOutcome: The component will display two interactive buttons for managing incidents, allowing users to simulate starting and resolving incidents.
successCriteria: Two button elements are added with correct text and onClick handlers wired to handleStartIncident and handleResolveIncident.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully added the incident control buttons. This completes the interactive incident management interface.
steps.feedbackPartial: You've added some buttons, but check that both buttons have the correct text and onClick handlers.
steps.feedbackWrong: The buttons are missing or incorrectly configured. Make sure to add two buttons with 'Start Incident' and 'Resolve Incident' text, each with onClick handlers.
